evidence_quotes.quote: The specific case involves a Paris-based water privatisation company (Suez) whose policies in Johannesburg led five Sowetans to sue the city to increase water supply and cease imposing pre-payment meters.
This article reviews the limits to a typical ‘rights-talk’ legalistic counterstrategy favoured by liberal non-governmental organisations (NGOs).
Nevertheless, this article draws on the 2008 to 2009 courtroom dramas to argue that a rights discourse has significant limitations so long as it remains primarily focused on the social domain.

As for the payment system, unlike conventional meters in wealthy suburbs, which provide due warning of future disconnection (and an opportunity to make representation), pre-payment meter disconnection occurs automatically and without warning following the exhaustion of the 6,000 litre free water supply.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and community water and sanitation service access in post-apartheid South Africa, focusing on Johannesburg and Soweto (Phiri), including Free Basic Water provision, prepayment water meters, disconnections, and low-cost sanitation technologies.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies both readings in subject matter. Under the plain wording, it examines constitutional and statutory water rights (South African Constitution s 27(1)(b), Water Services Act 108 of 1997), municipal water governance, and the Mazibuko litigation. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism clarification, it directly discusses tariff and cost-recovery rules (100% cost-recovery, convex rising block tariffs, Free Basic Water volume thresholds), eligibility screening and administrative burden (indigency registers and means testing), enforcement/credit-control mechanisms (prepayment water meters with automatic self-disconnection), and utility management contracting (Suez). However, these mechanisms are only discussed in a normative commentary rather than analysed empirically.
criterion_notes.c3: Fails Criterion 3 (E05). This law-journal article is a normative, theoretical, and political-economy commentary essay critiquing human-rights advocacy narratives ('rights-talk') versus a 'commons' framing in South African water struggles and global climate justice activism. It presents no primary empirical data, states no empirical data-collection or analytical methodology (quantitative, qualitative, or socio-legal empirical), and is not a systematic empirical synthesis; it relies solely on narrative discussion of secondary literature, press statements, and judicial opinions in Mazibuko v City of Johannesburg.
criterion_notes.c4: Discusses access-relevant outcomes—including household water disconnections, automatic suspension/self-disconnection via prepayment meters, free basic water quantity (25, 42, or 50 litres per person per day; 6kl or 10kl per household per month), and tariff affordability—using secondary sources and litigation records, without original empirical measurement.
criterion_notes.c5: No identifiable empirical study design, sample, or analytical unit of analysis is present because the article is a theoretical and normative essay rather than an empirical study.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is in English, an eligible language without translation.

exposure: Constitutional/statutory water rights framing, municipal water commercialisation (Suez management contract), rising block tariffs, indigency register/means testing, and prepayment water meters
outcome: Household water disconnections, prepayment meter self-disconnection, free basic water quantity, and tariff affordability (narrative/secondary discussion only)
rationale: Excluded under E05 (No empirical evidence). Although the article discusses household water and sanitation access in Johannesburg (c1) and rule-type legal/administrative mechanisms such as rising block tariffs, Free Basic Water allocations, indigency means testing, prepayment water meters, and utility management contracting (c2), it is a normative and theoretical commentary essay critiquing human-rights advocacy narratives ('rights-talk') in favour of a 'commons' framing across water and climate justice movements. It reports no primary data, has no empirical methodology or identifiable study design, and is not a systematic empirical synthesis.
